paragraphs: This paper studies how a group of agents can learn which choices give the best average reward when communication links appear randomly. The same choice can have different reward distributions for different agents, so each agent's local experience tells only part of the story. The objective is to perform well against rewards averaged across the entire group.

The proposed algorithm combines arm elimination, which discards choices judged unpromising, with random gossip, which spreads information between agents. Communication follows a fixed connected base network, but each possible link is independently available with probability p. Consequently, the network need not be connected at every step. Reward distributions remain fixed over time.

The theoretical regret bound grows logarithmically with the time horizon. It separates a centralized learning term from an additional communication term involving group size, the number of choices, link availability, and base-network connectivity. This makes the cost of unreliable communication explicit. A nearly optimal lower bound and numerical experiments further support the analysis and its predicted scaling.
neurips-2025-distributed-multi-agent-ban.tldr: A distributed bandit algorithm achieves logarithmic regret while explicitly accounting for random communication failures and differing rewards across agents.

paragraphs: Learning a useful robot policy involves both achieving goals and respecting safety constraints. This paper considers offline reinforcement learning, where training uses a fixed dataset instead of gathering experience through new interactions. That setting is valuable when exploratory actions could be unsafe, but the learner still has to reconcile reward maximization with limits on costly behavior.

The proposed method, DRCORL, first trains a diffusion model to capture the behavior represented in the dataset. It then extracts a simpler policy for efficient inference. A further gradient manipulation step adapts learning to safety requirements, balancing the reward objective against constraint satisfaction. The approach therefore combines a rich model of recorded behavior with a policy intended to be practical to execute.

Across the reported robot learning tasks, DRCORL achieves strong rewards, fast inference, and reliable safety performance. It consistently meets cost limits in comparisons with existing safe offline methods and works well with the same hyperparameters. These empirical results support its practical promise within the tested settings, while the approach explicitly draws on high-quality offline data.
neurips-2025-dont-trade-off-safety-diffu.tldr: DRCORL combines diffusion-based behavior modeling, policy simplification, and safety adaptation to achieve strong rewards while meeting cost limits in robot learning experiments.

paragraphs: This paper examines transformer token representations as objects that evolve under a dynamical system. It analyzes a continuous-time limit of a pretrained model to understand how representations behave over time. The central questions concern whether tokens move closer together or farther apart, and how those tendencies depend on model parameters.

The analysis gives sufficient parameter-based conditions for two extreme behaviors: representations converging to zero or diverging to infinity. Sufficient conditions identify cases where a behavior follows; they do not establish that every case with that behavior must meet those conditions. The authors describe their conditions as broader and more applicable to real models than earlier results. They also examine how absolute and rotary positional encodings affect these regimes.

Empirical evidence links the convergence scenario to poorer model performance. Motivated by that finding, the authors propose simple architectural refinements that mitigate convergence in transformers using either positional encoding. The contribution connects a mathematical account of representation dynamics with concrete design changes, using the observed performance consequences to guide architectural choices.
neurips-2025-dynamical-properties-of-tok.tldr: An analysis of transformer token dynamics identifies sufficient conditions for convergence or divergence and motivates architectural changes that mitigate harmful convergence.

paragraphs: Embodied AI systems can perceive, learn about, and act in the physical world. As their capabilities expand, their effects extend beyond the information they produce. This paper argues that their potential benefits come with risks requiring urgent policy attention, including physical harm, surveillance, and broader economic and social disruption.

The authors organize these concerns into a taxonomy covering physical, informational, economic, and social risks. They then examine policy frameworks in the United States, United Kingdom, and European Union to assess coverage and identify gaps. This structure connects different kinds of possible harm to the question of whether existing governance arrangements adequately address them.

The paper concludes that policies developed for industrial robots and autonomous vehicles do not cover the full range of embodied AI concerns. Its recommendations include mandatory testing and certification, clearer liability frameworks, and strategies for managing potentially transformative economic and societal effects. The contribution is a policy framework for anticipating and governing deployment, grounded in a structured risk analysis and comparison of existing approaches.
neurips-2025-emerging-risks-from-embodie.tldr: The paper maps embodied AI risks, identifies gaps in US, UK, and EU policies, and recommends stronger testing, liability, and societal planning.

paragraphs: A dynamical system can have several stable states, with its starting condition determining which state it approaches. Separatrices are the boundaries between those regions of attraction. Finding them matters because crossing a boundary can change a system's eventual behavior, yet these boundaries are difficult to characterize when the system has many dimensions.

The authors combine Koopman theory with deep neural networks to approximate particular scalar functions of the system state. These Koopman eigenfunctions have real positive eigenvalues and vanish at the separatrices. This turns boundary finding into an optimization problem involving scalar quantities, giving a numerical route to locating boundaries in complex systems.

The framework is demonstrated on synthetic examples, ecological networks, and high-dimensional recurrent neural networks trained on neuroscience-inspired tasks or fitted to neural data. The authors also use it to design optimal perturbations that move a system across a separatrix. That application connects the mathematical boundaries to predictions relevant to optogenetic stimulation experiments, where an intervention could redirect subsequent neural dynamics.
neurips-2025-finding-separatrices-of-dyn.tldr: Neural approximations of Koopman eigenfunctions help locate boundaries between dynamical outcomes and design perturbations that cross them.

paragraphs: Some control objectives describe behavior that must unfold over time rather than a single successful endpoint. Linear Temporal Logic provides a language for such objectives, including those extending over an infinite horizon. Existing approaches can translate these objectives into an automaton and reward scheme, but rewards tied to its accepting states are sparse, making useful exploration difficult.

This paper uses finite demonstrations to help agents reach those important states. It divides both demonstrations and the agent's exploratory trajectories into segments at accepting states of a Limit Deterministic Büchi Automaton. Learning then proceeds by repeatedly guiding the agent within each segment toward an accepting state.

The method encourages reaching accepting states from arbitrary states, increasing the probability of satisfying the temporal specification without requiring extensive or very long demonstrations. Its significance is that finite examples can help with an exploration problem arising from infinite-horizon objectives. Experiments across high-dimensional continuous control domains report faster convergence and consistent improvements over baseline approaches.
neurips-2025-imitation-learning-with-tem.tldr: Segmenting finite demonstrations around automaton accepting states helps control agents learn infinite-horizon temporal objectives more efficiently.

paragraphs: Understanding a video requires connecting events across frames. A model may recognize objects or write a brief caption while still failing to understand a continuous action or an object's transformation. This paper investigates those failures through language and image priors: tendencies that can support plausible answers without adequately using temporal relationships.

The proposed method changes decoding rather than adding a new training stage. It deliberately disrupts temporal consistency in key frames, causing the model to produce responses that are insensitive to the actual time structure. Those responses provide a contrast that guides generation away from the same kinds of errors when producing the final answer.

The central idea is to use the model's response to corrupted temporal evidence to encourage better use of coherent evidence. This offers a way to improve temporal reasoning without the additional training cost associated with retraining strategies. Experiments report consistent gains on both benchmarks targeting temporal reasoning and broader video understanding benchmarks, supporting the method's usefulness across the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2025-improve-temporal-reasoning-.tldr: Contrasting responses to temporally corrupted video frames improves video reasoning during decoding without additional training.

paragraphs: Many methods for aligning language models assume that each prompt-response pair has an underlying reward value that explains human preferences. The paper argues that this Bradley-Terry assumption can be too restrictive for complex preferences. It instead studies alignment through a two-player game, allowing a more general preference formulation.

The authors incorporate optimistic online mirror descent, drawing on methods for learning in games, to approximate a Nash policy. The theoretical analysis establishes a duality-gap bound that decreases as one over the number of iterations, improving on a previous inverse-square-root bound. The duality gap measures how far the learned solution remains from the game-theoretic target.

The paper also establishes linear convergence for the last iterate, giving a convergence result for the current policy itself. Beyond these theoretical properties, the authors implement the method and report stronger performance than state-of-the-art RLHF algorithms across several representative benchmarks. Together, the results connect a less restrictive preference model with faster theoretical convergence and empirical alignment improvements.
neurips-2025-improving-llm-general-prefe.tldr: A game-based alignment method handles general preferences and improves both theoretical convergence rates and reported benchmark performance.

paragraphs: Selecting a diverse subset can leave some members of a dataset poorly represented. This paper combines diversity maximization with an individual fairness requirement: every point should have a selected representative among its n/k nearest neighbors, where n is the dataset size and k is the number selected. Representation is therefore judged relative to each point's local neighborhood.

The authors develop approximation algorithms for three common diversity objectives: max-min, max-sum, and sum-min diversification. Their guarantees allow controlled compromises on both goals. Every point receives a representative within three times its distance to its n/k-th nearest neighbor, while the selected subset's diversity stays within a constant factor of the optimal value.

This is a bicriteria guarantee because it bounds both the relaxation of fairness and the loss in diversity. It does not promise exact satisfaction of the original nearest-neighbor requirement. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets show fairer representation than unconstrained algorithms, with only modest diversity losses, illustrating how the two goals can be balanced in practice.
neurips-2025-individually-fair-diversity.tldr: The paper gives diversity-selection algorithms with constant-factor diversity guarantees and a threefold relaxation of an individual representation requirement.

paragraphs: Steering guides a language model's behavior through an adjustment to its internal representations. Many existing approaches apply the same adjustment to every input. This paper argues that such a fixed direction can be inadequate for multimodal models, because the appropriate response depends on the particular example and the behavior being requested.

The authors investigate input-specific linear shifts derived from contrasting prompts tailored to each example. Those tailored prompts are unavailable at test time, so directly relying on them would not provide a usable inference procedure. Learn-to-Steer, or L2S, addresses this by training a small auxiliary module to predict the appropriate steering vector from the input.

This design allows the intervention to vary with context. For safety, the abstract distinguishes situations calling for abstention from those calling for external resources or expert consultation. The reported evaluation finds reduced hallucinations and improved enforcement of safety behavior compared with static steering baselines. The findings support input-dependent steering as a practical direction for guiding multimodal models.
neurips-2025-learning-to-steer-input-dep.tldr: L2S learns to predict input-specific steering vectors, improving hallucination and safety behavior over static interventions in multimodal models.

paragraphs: When several customers contribute preferences to a shared language-model fine-tuning service, they may benefit from misrepresenting what they want. That strategic behavior can undermine preference aggregation. This paper treats the service as a mechanism design problem in which the provider chooses both a training objective and a payment rule.

The analysis focuses on training rules that maximize social welfare subject to regularization. The authors show that, under most circumstances, such a rule alone does not make truthful reporting optimal. They extend VCG payments so that truthful reporting becomes a dominant strategy: an agent benefits from honesty regardless of how others report their preferences.

The paper also establishes sufficient conditions for payment equivalence and necessary conditions for payment rules to implement the desired training rules under incentive and other principles. With perturbed inputs, the mechanism is approximately dominant-strategy incentive compatible, addressing errors that can arise in practice. Experiments using real language-model training results support the practical implications of coupling preference aggregation with carefully designed payments.
neurips-2025-mechanism-design-for-llm-fi.tldr: Payment mechanisms can make honest preference reporting a dominant strategy for customers sharing an LLM fine-tuning service.

paragraphs: When observations are expensive, searching an environment requires choosing where to look next. DiffATD addresses this problem under a fixed sampling budget and partial observability. Its aim is to discover targets efficiently using information accumulated during the search, without requiring prior supervised training.

The method uses diffusion dynamics and maintains a belief distribution over each unobserved state. It balances two purposes for sampling: reducing uncertainty and finding likely targets. Exploration favors regions with the highest expected entropy, while exploitation uses target likelihoods from the belief distribution together with a reward model that learns target characteristics incrementally.

This explicit separation of uncertainty and target likelihood also gives an interpretable account of sampling decisions. The authors evaluate the method through experiments and ablations across medical imaging, species discovery, and remote sensing. They report significant improvements over baselines and competitive performance with supervised methods that have full environmental observability. The results suggest that adaptive use of online feedback can make limited observations productive across the tested domains.
neurips-2025-online-feedback-efficient-a.tldr: DiffATD balances uncertainty reduction and target likelihood to guide budget-limited searches without prior supervised training.

paragraphs: Generative models can produce solutions for physical systems described by partial differential equations, but plausible outputs can still violate physical requirements. Conservation laws and other consistency conditions may need to hold exactly. The paper addresses the difficulty of enforcing these hard constraints when soft penalties or architectural biases do not guarantee compliance.

Physics-Constrained Flow Matching, or PCFM, operates at inference time on pretrained flow-based generative models. It applies physics-based corrections to intermediate solution states throughout sampling, while keeping the process aligned with the learned flow. The framework is presented as zero-shot and supports arbitrary nonlinear constraints, allowing constraint enforcement without a new training stage.

Experiments cover several PDEs, including cases with shocks, discontinuities, and sharp features. PCFM outperforms both constrained and unconstrained baselines in the reported evaluation and ensures exact constraint satisfaction in the final solution. The contribution combines learned generation with explicit physical correction, providing a route to using generative models where final outputs must obey specified constraints.
neurips-2025-physics-constrained-flow-ma.tldr: PCFM corrects pretrained flow-model samples during inference to enforce hard physical constraints, with exact final constraint satisfaction in reported PDE experiments.

paragraphs: Robotic manipulation benefits from both geometric and visual information. Point clouds describe spatial structure, while RGB images provide semantic context. The paper identifies complementary weaknesses in existing approaches: point-cloud methods can miss fine detail, and image-based methods lack geometric awareness needed for precise and generalizable behavior.

PointMapPolicy conditions diffusion policies on point maps, which arrange 3D points in structured grids without downsampling. This preserves detailed observations while making shape and spatial relationships easier to extract. The maps can also be transformed between reference frames. Their regular grid structure enables established computer vision techniques to operate directly on the 3D information.

An xLSTM backbone fuses the point maps with RGB data, combining geometry and appearance within the policy's perception system. The authors evaluate the approach on RoboCasa, CALVIN, and real robots, reporting state-of-the-art performance across diverse manipulation tasks. The results support the usefulness of the chosen representation: structured 3D observations can retain detail while fitting naturally into techniques for processing visual data.
neurips-2025-pointmappolicy-structured-p.tldr: PointMapPolicy combines full-resolution structured 3D point grids with RGB observations to improve diffusion policies for robotic manipulation.

paragraphs: A generated Verilog module can be partly wrong while still implementing some output signals correctly. Evaluating only whether the entire module works discards that useful partial success. QiMeng-SALV uses correctly implemented signals inside otherwise incorrect modules to obtain more meaningful functional feedback for training code-generating language models.

The method compares generated signals with a reference module from the training data to verify their behavior. It then uses the code's abstract syntax tree to identify the segments associated with correct signals. A signal-aware form of direct preference optimization trains on those segments, avoiding noise and interference from incorrect outputs.

The main contribution is a finer unit of optimization: functional signal implementations rather than whole modules. This makes partially successful generations useful training evidence. Experiments report state-of-the-art performance on VerilogEval and RTLLM. A 7B-parameter model matches the performance of DeepSeek v3's 671B model in the reported evaluation and significantly outperforms CodeV trained on the same dataset, supporting the value of more precise functional feedback.
neurips-2025-qimeng-salv-signal-aware-le.tldr: QiMeng-SALV improves Verilog generation by training on verified signal-level code extracted from partially incorrect modules.

paragraphs: Binary classification becomes especially difficult when one class is rare, the dataset is small, and each example has many features. Noisy features can encourage overfitting, while the scarce minority examples give the learner little evidence about that class. QuanDA is designed for this combination of imbalance and high dimensionality.

The method builds discriminant analysis around a connection to quantile regression. By choosing appropriate quantile levels, it incorporates class imbalance into the classification approach itself. The authors provide a theoretical analysis supporting the method in ultra-high-dimensional settings, addressing the statistical challenge created by having many potential predictors and limited observations.

The evaluation combines simulations with analyses of high-dimensional benchmark datasets. QuanDA performs better overall than the compared approaches, including cost-sensitive large-margin classifiers, random forests, and SMOTE. The qualification 'overall' matters: the stated finding concerns the combined experimental picture. The work's significance is to connect an imbalance-aware statistical formulation with both theoretical support and empirical evidence in settings where rare classes are difficult to detect.
neurips-2025-quanda-quantile-based-discr.tldr: QuanDA uses quantile-based discriminant analysis to address class imbalance in small-sample, high-dimensional classification.

paragraphs: Spiking Transformers aim to combine efficient spike-based computation with self-attention's representational power. Comparing these models is difficult when implementations, evaluation procedures, and design choices differ. STEP provides a shared framework intended to make those comparisons fairer and the resulting findings easier to reproduce.

The platform supports classification, segmentation, and detection on static, event-based, and sequential data. Its modular components include neuron types, input encodings, surrogate gradients, and multiple software backends. The authors reproduce representative models and systematically vary attention designs, neurons, encodings, and temporal modeling components to examine what contributes to performance.

STEP also introduces an analytical energy model that accounts for spike sparsity, numerical bitwidth, and memory access. Under this analysis, quantized conventional neural networks may match or exceed spiking models' energy efficiency. The experiments further suggest that current Spiking Transformers depend heavily on convolutional frontends and have weak temporal modeling. These findings motivate architectures designed more directly around spike-based computation, while qualifying broad assumptions about existing models' efficiency.
neurips-2025-step-a-unified-spiking-tran.tldr: STEP standardizes Spiking Transformer evaluation and finds that current designs may offer limited temporal modeling and no clear energy advantage over quantized networks.

paragraphs: Frame interpolation generates an intermediate view of motion from input video frames. A central difficulty is matching the same objects between frames when they move substantially. This paper argues that estimating correspondences in two-dimensional image space limits existing approaches, because real-world motion occurs in three dimensions.

The proposed pipeline first transforms a pair of frames from image coordinates into a differential surface coordinate system. It then searches for object correspondences using surface geometry and the surface uniqueness theorem. The change of representation is intended to make the geometric structure of the scene more useful for matching objects across the two observations.

The significance lies in where correspondence reasoning takes place: the method introduces surface structure into a problem that is often handled within image coordinates. The reported experiments achieve state-of-the-art performance on large-motion frame interpolation benchmarks and subsets. Those findings support the proposed geometric representation for the particular difficulty emphasized by the paper, namely maintaining useful object correspondences when motion between frames is large.
neurips-2025-surface-aware-feed-forward-.tldr: A surface-coordinate representation improves object matching for frame interpolation and achieves state-of-the-art results on large-motion evaluations.

paragraphs: Compressing information exchanged during distributed learning can reduce communication costs, but compression can also slow convergence. Error feedback methods compensate for compression errors, aiming to preserve learning progress while sending less information. This paper provides a tight theoretical analysis of two prominent methods, EF and EF21.

The authors identify a Lyapunov function for each method that yields its best possible convergence rate in the analyzed setting. A Lyapunov function provides a way to track progress as optimization proceeds. Matching lower bounds establish the tightness of the resulting rates, making the guarantees more informative than bounds that might leave substantial room for improvement.

The common analytical treatment enables a rigorous comparison of EF, EF21, and compressed gradient descent. Although communication in distributed learning motivates the work, the analysis deliberately uses a simplified single-agent setting. That scope allows the underlying compression and correction mechanisms to be compared cleanly. The contribution is therefore sharper understanding of these mechanisms and their convergence guarantees within that setting.
neurips-2025-tight-analyses-of-first-ord.tldr: Tight single-agent analyses of EF and EF21 establish matching convergence bounds and enable a principled comparison of compression methods.

paragraphs: Self-attention is effective, but its underlying optimization purpose can be unclear and its quadratic cost becomes expensive as inputs grow. This paper treats interpretability and efficiency as related design goals. It proposes an explicit optimization objective and derives an attention mechanism whose operations implement a gradient step for that objective.

The resulting Contract-and-Broadcast Self-Attention, or CBSA, compresses token representations toward low-dimensional structures by contracting a small set of representative tokens. Algorithm unrolling connects this mathematical update to the model's forward computation. When the number of representatives stays fixed, the mechanism scales linearly with the number of input tokens.

Different choices of representatives also recover instances of varied attention mechanisms, giving the framework a unifying role. Experiments on visual tasks report comparable performance and advantages over the evaluated black-box attention mechanisms. The central contribution is the connection between computation and objective: the same construction explains what an attention update is doing and provides a condition under which its cost scales more favorably.
neurips-2025-towards-interpretable-and-e.tldr: CBSA derives attention from an explicit optimization objective and achieves linear scaling when its number of representative tokens is fixed.

paragraphs: Supervised fine-tuning normally uses generation errors to update a model's parameters. Transformer Copilot also retains information about how those errors evolve. Its Mistake Log tracks learning behavior and recurring mistakes throughout fine-tuning, turning the training process into an additional source of information for improving later predictions.

The framework calls the original transformer the Pilot and trains a companion Copilot alongside it. The Copilot continuously learns from the evolving Mistake Log. During inference, the two models operate together: the Copilot adjusts the Pilot's logits, the scores used to determine generated outputs. This connects observed training mistakes to a direct intervention in prediction.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical analyses and evaluate the framework on 12 benchmarks covering commonsense, arithmetic, and recommendation tasks. They report consistent improvements, reaching up to 34.5%, with marginal computational overhead for the Pilot models. They also report strong scalability and transferability. The maximum improvement describes the upper end of the reported gains, while the broader finding supports learning from retained error patterns.
neurips-2025-transformer-copilot-learnin.tldr: Transformer Copilot learns from a model's evolving training mistakes and adjusts its output scores to improve inference.

paragraphs: Visual Jenga asks a scene-understanding system to remove objects from a single image one at a time until only the background remains. The challenge is to preserve physical and geometric coherence throughout the sequence. Choosing a sensible removal order therefore requires understanding dependencies between objects, beyond merely identifying what is present.

The paper introduces a training-free approach that uses a large inpainting model to generate counterfactual versions of the scene. These imagined alternatives help quantify asymmetry in pairwise object relationships. An asymmetric relationship means that the consequences of removing one object differ from the consequences of removing the other, providing evidence about their dependency.

The authors report that this simple, data-driven approach is effective on a range of real-world images. Its contribution includes both a new task and an initial method for addressing it. The broader idea is to investigate scene relationships through controlled visual changes: testing which removals preserve coherence can reveal structure that is difficult to capture through object recognition alone.
neurips-2025-visual-jenga-discovering-ob.tldr: Visual Jenga uses counterfactual inpainting to infer object dependencies and remove scene elements in a physically and geometrically coherent order.

paragraphs: Generating new viewpoints from one image requires preserving visible details while inventing plausible content for previously hidden regions. In 3D GAN inversion, an encoder maps the image into a pretrained generator's latent space. The paper identifies a weakness in relying on that compact latent code and the generator's prior alone to reconstruct unseen content.

WarpGAN adds a warping-and-inpainting process. After encoding the input, it uses a depth map produced by the 3D GAN to warp image content into the requested viewpoint. Its SVINet component then fills occluded regions using a symmetry prior and correspondences between views associated with the same latent code.

This design gives hidden-region generation additional structure from image relationships and symmetry. It addresses the need for unseen content to look realistic while remaining consistent across viewpoints, alongside faithful reconstruction of visible regions. Quantitative and qualitative experiments report consistent improvements over several state-of-the-art methods. The findings support combining geometric transfer of observed content with a dedicated mechanism for completing what the new view exposes.
neurips-2025-warpgan-warping-guided-3d-g.tldr: WarpGAN combines depth-guided warping with symmetry- and correspondence-based inpainting to improve new views generated from a single image.

paragraphs: This paper uses the Andrews-Curtis conjecture from combinatorial group theory as a case study of difficult reinforcement learning problems. Its focus is the search for rare instances that carry unusually high rewards. Such a setting puts the relationship between mathematical problem difficulty and an agent's ability to find valuable outcomes at the center of the investigation.

The authors examine the challenge from multiple perspectives and analyze how reinforcement learning agents handle problems of varying hardness within this mathematical context. The study also addresses mathematical questions directly. This gives the work two connected purposes: investigating learning behavior and advancing understanding of the concrete instances used in that investigation.

The stated mathematical results include length reducibility for all but two presentations in the Akbulut-Kirby series and resolution of several potential counterexamples in the Miller-Schupp series, including three infinite subfamilies. These are specific advances within the case study, rather than a claimed resolution of the overall conjecture. They provide substantive mathematical outcomes alongside the examination of rare-reward search.
neurips-2025-what-makes-math-problems-ha.tldr: A group-theory case study examines reinforcement learning on rare-reward problems while resolving specific mathematical instances and infinite subfamilies.

paragraphs: Learning to generate new views of whole scenes is difficult when clean multi-view training data are scarce. Photographs collected in the wild offer more diversity, but their lighting, temporary occlusions, and other appearance conditions vary. WildCAT3D aims to make these abundant scene images usable for learning novel-view generation.

The framework extends multi-view diffusion by explicitly modeling global appearance conditions. This lets training account for appearance changes between scene views instead of requiring uniformly captured images. At inference time, the trained model generalizes to new scenes and can generate multiple consistent views. It also permits control over global appearance during generation.

The authors report state-of-the-art single-view novel-view synthesis results in both object-centered and scene-level settings while using strictly fewer training data sources than previous methods. That claim concerns the number of sources, rather than establishing a smaller total image count. The contribution connects broader use of varied real-world imagery with consistent viewpoint generation and an additional means of controlling the resulting appearance.
neurips-2025-wildcat3d-appearance-aware-.tldr: WildCAT3D models appearance variation to learn consistent novel-view generation from diverse scene photos collected in the wild.
